incidents.cause: A reported partial loss of engine power for undetermined reasons.
The in-flight collision with a tree while returning to land for undetermined reasons.
The pilot's failure to attain the proper touchdown point.
The pilot’s inadequate use of carburetor heat during the engine run-up, which resulted in a partial loss of power due to carburetor icing during takeoff.
The pilot’s flight in dark night conditions with no visual reference and his subsequent spatial disorientation.
Deformation of the No. 1 cylinder's intake valve, which resulted in a partial loss of engine power and a subsequent off-airport precautionary landing.

The pilot's failure to use the mixture control to override a throttle anomaly and reduce engine power, which resulted in excessive airspeed upon landing and a subsequent runway overrun. The student pilot's improper decision to conduct a flight in dark night conditions without a solo night flight endorsement and his subsequent loss of airplane control.
The pilot’s improper fuel management, which resulted in a loss of engine power due to fuel starvation.
The pilot's inadequate decision to continue the approach, which resulted in a  long landing and insufficient runway remaining to stop the airplane before it departed the end of the runway.

The pilot’s failure to maintain airspeed during takeoff, which resulted in an aerodynamic stall. Contributing to the accident was the airplane’s reduced climb performance due to density altitude, as well as the pilot’s decision to initiate the takeoff from the wet turf runway.
The airplane’s degraded performance from the rough, grass runway surface and the pilot’s delayed decision to abort the takeoff resulting in a runway excursion.
A total loss of engine power for undetermined reasons.
An in-flight collision with a bird during low-altitude maneuvering, which resulted in a hard landing.
The solo student pilot's improper cyclic input during takeoff, which resulted in dynamic rollover.

The flight instructor’s delayed remedial action and inadequate supervision during a practice autorotation, which resulted in a failure to maintain adequate main rotor rpm. Contributing to the accident was the wet landing surface.
The flight instructor's failure to maintain control of the helicopter during an autorotation, which resulted in a hard landing.
The student pilot's improper cyclic input while hovering and the flight instructor's delayed remedial action, which resulted in a dynamic rollover.

The pilot’s decision to takeoff from a contaminated runway with unfavorable wind conditions, and his failure to maintain airspeed during the initial climb, which resulted in an aerodynamic stall. A total loss of engine power due to the fatigue failure of the crankshaft, which resulted from improper tightening of the cylinder hold-down nuts.

The pilot's loss of directional control during the landing roll for reasons that could not be determined, because postaccident examination of the nosewheel assembly revealed no anomalies that would have precluded normal operation.
The pilot’s failure to remain clear of rising terrain while maneuvering at low altitude.
The total loss of engine power for an undetermined reason.
The pilot’s failure to maintain an appropriate descent rate for a glassy water landing, which resulted in a hard landing.
The pilot's decision to conduct a precautionary landing following a loss of altitude during takeoff initial climb.

The pilot's improper decision to takeoff in an area of rough water and ocean swells, which resulted in a failure of the right float struts.

A total loss of engine power due to air entering the fuel system for reasons that could not be determined based on available information.  Contributing to the accident was the pilot’s inability to restart the engine due to the check valve assembly design.
The pilot's misjudged speed and distance during takeoff, which resulted in the float-equipped airplane colliding with a bank.
The loss of engine power for an undetermined reason, resulting in an off-airport emergency landing and subsequent nose over.
The airplane’s float contacted an undetected submerged gravel bar during landing which resulted in a nose over.

The pilot's failure to maintain adequate airspeed during the initial climb after taking off from a wet runway and his exceedance of the airplane’s critical angle of attack, which resulted in an aerodynamic stall.

The inadequate visual lookout and failure to see and avoid by the pilots of both airplanes while maneuvering to land, which resulted in a midair collision. The flight crew’s failure to ensure that the landing gear were properly configured before landing.
The pilot's misidentification of the runway surface during landing. Contributing to the accident were the snow-covered terrain, and low-light conditions.
The pilot’s descent below glidepath, which resulted in the airplane’s impact with power lines.
The pilot's failure to maintain directional control during the landing roll, which resulted in a runway excursion and a nose over.

The student pilot's failure to establish a positive climb rate during an aborted landing, which resulted in abnormal runway contact, a subsequent loss of directional control, runway excursion, and the right main landing gear collapsing.
The pilot’s selection of unsuitable terrain for landing, which resulted in a loss of directional control and subsequent nose-over.
The pilot’s failure to avoid an obstacle during his approach to land.
The pilot’s improper compensation for shifting wind conditions, which resulted in a runway excursion and a subsequent nose over.
The pilot's failure to select the proper fuel tank before departure, which resulted in fuel starvation and a total loss of engine power.
The mechanical failure of the left main landing gear leg due to corrosion, resulting in substantial damage to the left struts.

The total loss of engine power for reasons that could not be determined because postaccident examination of the engine revealed no mechanical malfunctions or failures that would have precluded normal operation. The pilot’s failure to maintain directional control while landing in a crosswind.
The pilot’s exceedance of the airplane’s critical angle of attack during the landing flare, which resulted in an aerodynamic stall.

The total loss of engine power during the initial climb due to fuel contamination. Contributing to the accident was the corrosion of the fuel tank filler necks, which resulted in water intrusion into the fuel tanks.
The pilot's failure to maintain directional control while landing with a crosswind.
The pilot’s failure to maintain clearance from terrain while maneuvering at low altitude.
The pilot's failure to maintain directional control while taking off in known gusty wind conditions.
The pilot's improper landing flare and inadequate recovery from a bounced landing.
The pilot’s improper recovery from a bounced landing.
Oil starvation that led to the failure of the No. 5 connecting rod and a subsequent loss of engine power.
The pilot’s failure to maintain directional control during initial climb following a banner pick-up, resulting in collision with a tree.
A failure of the nose wheel steering shaft and subsequent rotation of the nosewheel which resulted in the collapse of the nose landing gear during landing.
The pilot’s improper landing flare, which resulted in a hard, bounced landing.
The fatigue failure of the left main landing gear due to inadequate maintenance inspection that did not detect and correct corrosion pitting.
The pilot’s failure to maintain directional control while landing with a gusting crosswind.
The pilot’s failure to secure the left-wing fuel cap after refueling the airplane, which resulted in a fuel leak on takeoff.
A partial loss of engine power for reasons that could not be determined due to the available evidence.
The pilot's failure to perform a go-around in time to prevent a runway overrun and collision with terrain.
A fire of undetermined origin.
The pilot’s failure to maintain control while landing in a gusting wind.
A failed main landing gear tire for reasons that could not be determined due to postcrash fire damage.
The pilot's improper landing flare, which resulted in a bounced landing and subsequent ground loop.
The pilot’s loss of situational awareness during the approach over a corn field, which resulted in collision with corn stalks.
The pilot's failure to attain a proper approach speed, which resulted in an overrun of the wet grass runway.
The pilot’s failure to maintain directional control during the landing roll with a tailwind.
The pilot’s failure to maintain directional control during landing.
The flight instructor’s improper landing flare and failure to maintain a proper descent rate during approach, which resulted in a hard landing.

The pilot's failure to follow the airplane's operating limitations by rapidly opening the throttle, which resulted in a loss of engine power. Contributing to the accident was the pilot's decision to maneuver the airplane at low altitude even though he was not taking off or landing.
The pilot's delayed action to abort the takeoff. Contributing to the accident was the pilot's inadequate preflight planning and a high density altitude.
The pilot's inadequate preflight inspection, which resulted in an inflight fire due to the presence of a bird nest in the engine compartment.
The pilot’s improper use of the fuel selector, which resulted in fuel starvation to the engine and an off-runway landing.
The student pilot’s loss of directional control during the landing roll and his subsequent inadvertent brake application, which resulted in a nose-over.
The pilot’s failure to maintain directional control during the landing roll resulting in a ground loop.
